prompt: Which strategy helps reduce overflow/underflow occurrences?
explanation: Double precision widens the exponent from 8 bits to 11, which stretches the range from about 10 to the power plus or minus 38 out to about 10 to the power plus or minus 308.

why.a: Wrong. ASCII is a character code and performs no arithmetic at all.
why.b: Correct. More exponent bits means more range, so fewer results fall off either end.
why.c: Wrong, and exactly backwards. Fewer bits shrink the range and cause MORE overflow.
why.d: Wrong. BCD codes decimal digits and is less compact than binary, so it does not extend numeric range.

prompt: A banking application depends heavily on accurate decimal calculations. Which architectural feature directly influences calculation accuracy?
explanation: Accuracy is decided by how a number is REPRESENTED: how many mantissa bits hold the significant digits.

why.a: Correct. The mantissa width sets how many significant digits survive, which is precision itself.
why.b: Wrong. Cache changes how quickly data arrives, never what the computed value is.
why.c: Wrong. Control signals sequence the hardware. They do not alter numeric precision.
why.d: Wrong. A wider bus moves more bits per transfer, a speed matter and not an accuracy one.

prompt: Approximately what numeric range can IEEE Double Precision represent?
explanation: Double precision reaches roughly 10 to the power plus or minus 308. Learn it as a pair with single precision at roughly 10 to the power plus or minus 38, because this paper sets both.

why.a: Wrong. That is the SINGLE precision figure, the other half of the pair.
why.b: Wrong. 128 is close to the single precision exponent bias of 127, not a decimal range.
why.c: Correct. About 10 to the power plus or minus 308.
why.d: Wrong. 256 is a familiar power of two, put here to look plausible. It is not the figure.

explanation: Double precision is 64 bits: 1 sign, 11 exponent, 52 mantissa. Single precision is 32 bits: 1 sign, 8 exponent, 23 mantissa. Those two lines answer most floating-point questions on this paper.

why.b: Wrong. 32 bits is SINGLE precision, and the name double says twice that.
why.c: Wrong. 48 bits is not an IEEE 754 basic format.
why.d: Wrong. 128 bits is quadruple precision, which the course does not set.

prompt: A floating-point number is generally stored as:
explanation: Sign, Mantissa, Exponent is what the exam keyed, and it is the only option offered that puts the sign first. Know the truth as well: real IEEE 754 hardware lays the fields out as Sign, EXPONENT, Mantissa, and that ordering is not offered here. Take the keyed answer in this test, and write Sign, Exponent, Mantissa in a theory answer.

why.a: Wrong. The sign is always the leading bit, so it cannot come second.
why.b: Wrong. This puts the sign last, when it is in fact the first bit of the word.
why.c: Wrong. ASCII digits would store the number as text, which is not a floating-point format at all.
why.d: Correct as the paper keyed it, and the only answer offered that puts the sign first. Be aware that the true IEEE 754 order is Sign, Exponent, Mantissa, which this paper does not list.

prompt: What is the principal advantage of floating-point representation?

options.text: Representation of very large and very small values

explanation: A movable binary point buys enormous dynamic range in a fixed number of bits.

why.a: Wrong, and the opposite of the truth. Floating point is approximate: 0.1 cannot be stored exactly in binary.
why.b: Wrong. Floating-point arithmetic is generally SLOWER than integer arithmetic, since it must align exponents and normalise.
why.c: Wrong. The range is larger, not infinite, so overflow still occurs at the ends.
why.d: Correct. Huge and tiny magnitudes in the same fixed-width word, which is what dynamic range means.

prompt: A weather simulation program requires highly accurate numerical computations. Which architectural component is most critical?
explanation: Same rule as the banking question: when a stem says ACCURATE or PRECISE numerical work, the answer is floating-point representation. When it says FASTER, look to cache and organization instead.

why.a: Correct. Precision comes from the number format, and simulations accumulate error over millions of steps.
why.b: Wrong. A replacement policy affects hit rate and therefore speed, not the computed values.
why.c: Wrong. Character encoding is for text, and a simulation computes on numbers.
why.d: Wrong. The control bus carries command signals, which has no bearing on numerical accuracy.

prompt: Approximately what numeric range can IEEE Single Precision represent?
explanation: Single precision reaches roughly 10 to the power plus or minus 38.

why.a: Wrong. That is the DOUBLE precision figure, offered to catch a reader who learned only one of the pair.
why.b: Correct. About 10 to the power plus or minus 38 from 32 bits with an 8-bit exponent.
why.c: Wrong, far too small. 8 exponent bits reach well past 10 to the power 20.
why.d: Wrong, smaller still. That is roughly the range of a 32-bit integer, not of a float.

prompt: IEEE Single Precision allocates how many bits to the exponent?
explanation: Single precision is 1 + 8 + 23 = 32 bits, so the exponent takes 8.

why.a: Correct. 8 exponent bits, which is where the plus or minus 38 range comes from.
why.b: Wrong. 23 is the MANTISSA width of the same format.
why.c: Wrong. 7 bits is the width of an ASCII character, not of this exponent.
why.d: Wrong. 11 is the exponent width of DOUBLE precision.

prompt: The exponent bias used in IEEE Double Precision is:
explanation: The bias is 2 to the power (e minus 1), minus 1, where e is the exponent width. Double has 11 exponent bits, so the bias is 1024 minus 1 = 1023.

why.a: Wrong. 127 is the SINGLE precision bias, from 8 exponent bits.
why.b: Wrong. 255 is the largest value in 8 bits, not a bias.
why.c: Wrong. 511 would be the bias for a 10-bit exponent, and double uses 11.
why.d: Correct. 2 to the power 10, which is 1024, minus 1.
